events.description: US and Taliban sign the withdrawal agreement in Doha (host mis-speaks the year as 2000). The hosts say it has no reduction-in-violence, al-Qaeda-break or negotiation requirements.

Jake Sullivan states three conditions for Taliban compliance (cut ties with terrorists including al-Qaeda, reduce violence, negotiate with the Afghan government) and that the Biden administration is reviewing the deal.
Taliban statement calls the Doha deal a 'termination of occupation agreement'.
Taliban assassination campaign against civil society, including two female judges killed in Kabul, plus lawyers, politicians, journalists and NGO workers.
Taliban delegation travels to Russia; earlier meetings in Iran and a trip to Indonesia in recent weeks.
Obama administration walks away from talks with the Taliban partly because the Taliban refused to drop 'Islamic Emirate' language.
Trump plans to host the Taliban at Camp David; the Taliban released videos memorializing 9/11 and blaming the US.
Mike Pompeo, as the first US cabinet official to do so, meets the Taliban in Doha.
US Afghan surge, which the hosts criticized; they say more US soldiers were killed and wounded during it than in the rest of the war combined.
US-Taliban withdrawal agreement signed. The US is to withdraw by May 2021, the Taliban are to prevent al-Qaeda from using Afghan soil, and the US pledges no force against Afghanistan.
Hosts published a Politico article setting out specific criteria for a real Taliban break with al-Qaeda.
Afghan surge, which the hosts criticized and say caused heavy US casualties.
Deadline in the agreement for full US withdrawal (May 1, 2021).
US Treasury report to the Defense Department on Taliban, al-Qaeda and ISIS financing concluded al-Qaeda is gaining strength under the Taliban banner. The Taliban dismissed it as warmongering.
Three senior al-Qaeda leaders killed in the last year and a half, in Taliban-controlled areas and alongside Taliban leaders.
A joint Afghan-American raid in Helmand killed AQIS emir Asim Omar alongside Taliban commanders. The DOD reportedly buried the press release.
A US-confirmed killing of senior al-Qaeda figure Husam Abd al-Rauf ('Osama Roof') in Afghanistan, never tied publicly to the Taliban deal.
The US-Taliban (Doha) agreement; the hosts say the Taliban has not complied for more than 11 months.
Mullah Mansour was appointed Taliban leader after Mullah Omar's death was disclosed, causing a schism. Sirajuddin and Jalaluddin Haqqani helped bring the factions back together.
Pentagon spokesman Kirby said the Taliban is not living up to the deal and has not renounced terrorism or al-Qaeda.
National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan said the Taliban would have to renounce ties to al-Qaeda and other terrorist groups.

key_claims: The 29 Feb 2020 US-Taliban agreement contains no commitment to reduce violence, no real commitment to break with al-Qaeda, and no requirement to negotiate meaningfully with the Afghan government.
Taliban violence has risen significantly since the deal (estimates of 60-100%), and the Taliban are running an assassination campaign against judges, journalists, politicians and NGO workers.
The Taliban see the deal as ending the US occupation and plan to seize control of Afghanistan, with the Doha talks serving as show talks to run out the clock.
The Taliban's insistence on 'Islamic Emirate' language shows they have not abandoned their goal of resurrecting their authoritarian regime.
Khalilzad and the Trump administration gave the Taliban international legitimacy (Doha, Pompeo meeting, Camp David invitation, trips to Russia, Iran and Indonesia) without getting concessions.
US officials, including General Miller and Khalilzad, repeat talking points not found in the agreement, such as that the Taliban agreed to cut ties with al-Qaeda.
The Taliban have taken no action against al-Qaeda in the 11 months since the agreement; there have been zero Taliban raids killing or capturing al-Qaeda members.
The Taliban deny al-Qaeda is in Afghanistan even as US and Afghan raids kill and capture its leaders and al-Qaeda publicizes its operations there.
Al-Qaeda and the Taliban are inextricably entangled, so al-Qaeda cannot be fought in Afghanistan without fighting the Taliban.
The US Treasury concluded independently that al-Qaeda is gaining strength under the Taliban banner.
The agreement's language on al-Qaeda is generic, with no enforcement or verification, and it commits the US not to use force against Afghanistan.
The Haqqanis, with Sirajuddin as effective number two, hold a predominant share of the Taliban and are building a new force with al-Qaeda.
A Taliban takeover alongside al-Qaeda would boost global jihad and al-Qaeda's Pakistani networks, though a new 9/11 is not guaranteed.
The Taliban has not broken with al-Qaeda in the 11+ months since the Doha deal, so there is no reason to assume Afghanistan's problems stay in Afghanistan.
The Haqqani Network is a designated terrorist organization, closely allied with al-Qaeda, and holds a major share of the Taliban's operations and leadership.
Sirajuddin Haqqani, effectively the Taliban's number two, would have to publicly denounce al-Qaeda for the agreement to mean anything, which the hosts say will not happen.

Asim Omar, a direct courier to Zawahiri, was killed in Helmand in September 2019 in a Taliban compound under a Taliban shadow governor's protection, which is evidence of Taliban sheltering of al-Qaeda.
The DOD buried its press release on Asim Omar's killing and did not use that evidence against the Taliban in negotiations.
Al-Qaeda is embedded in Pakistani and Afghan jihadist groups, and a haven in Afghanistan would likely increase activity across the Indian subcontinent.
Fewer than 2,500 US troops cannot effectively target al-Qaeda, and more senior al-Qaeda leaders remain in Afghanistan beyond the three killed in the past year and a half.
